# 2 Maccabees Chapter 12 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 12 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_012_page_001.jpg

---

**12:1** When these agreements had been made, Lysias returned to the king, and the Jews went back to their farming.

**12:2** But certain of the local governors — Timothy, Apollonius son of Gennaeus, Hieronymus, and Demophon, and in addition Nicanor the governor of Cyprus — would not allow them to enjoy peace and quiet.

**12:3** The people of Joppa committed the following impiety: they invited the Jews who lived among them to embark, with their wives and children, on boats they had provided, giving no indication of any ill will,

**12:4** and when the Jews, trusting in the general decision of the city, agreed and went aboard, the Joppites took them out to sea and drowned them, no fewer than two hundred persons.

**12:5** When Judas learned what had been done to his compatriots, he gave orders to his men

**12:6** and, calling on God the just judge, marched against the murderers of his kinsmen. He set the harbor on fire by night, burned the boats, and put to the sword those who had taken refuge there.

**12:7** The town was closed against him, so he withdrew, intending to return and root out the entire population of Joppa.

**12:8** On learning that the people of Jamnia too were planning to act in the same manner against the Jews who lived among them,

**12:9** he attacked the Jamnites by night as well and set fire to the harbor and the fleet, so that the glow of the fire was visible in Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia away.

**12:10** When they had advanced nine stadia from there in their march against Timothy, no fewer than five thousand Arabs with five hundred horsemen attacked them.

**12:11** After a fierce battle in which God gave them his help, the nomads were overcome; and the Arabs, having been defeated, begged Judas for terms, promising to supply him with livestock and to assist him in other ways.

**12:12** Judas, judging that they would in truth prove useful to him in many respects, agreed to make peace with them; and after pledges had been exchanged they withdrew to their tents.

**12:13** He also attacked a certain city, Caspin by name, strongly fortified with ramparts and walls, and inhabited by a mixed population of various peoples.

**12:14** Those within, relying on the strength of the walls and their store of provisions, behaved insolently toward Judas and his men, insulting them with abusive words and saying things that were not lawful to utter.

**12:15** But Maccabeus, calling upon the great Sovereign of the world who, without battering rams or engines of war, had thrown down Jericho in the days of Joshua, launched himself fiercely against the wall.

**12:16** Taking the city by the will of God, he carried out a slaughter beyond all telling, so that the adjacent lake — two stadia wide — appeared to be overflowing with blood.

**12:17** From there they marched seven hundred and fifty stadia and came to Charax, to the Jews known as the Tubiani.

**12:18** They did not find Timothy in those parts; he had already withdrawn from the region without having accomplished anything, though he had left behind a very strong garrison at one position.

**12:19** Dositheus and Sosipater, who were commanders under Maccabeus, marched out and destroyed the force Timothy had left in the stronghold — more than ten thousand men.

**12:20** Maccabeus organized his army into divisions, placed these commanders over the divisions, and pressed his pursuit of Timothy, who had a hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred cavalry.

**12:21** On learning of Judas's approach, Timothy sent the women, the children, and the baggage to a place called Carnaim, which was hard to besiege and difficult to reach because of the constricted nature of the terrain at all its approaches.

**12:22** But when the first division of Judas appeared, the enemies were struck with terror and fear at the manifestation of him who sees all things, and they fled in utter rout in every direction, so that they were often hurt by their own men and impaled on the points of their own swords.

**12:23** Judas pressed the pursuit hard and put the criminals to the sword, destroying as many as thirty thousand men.

**12:24** Timothy himself fell into the hands of Dositheus and Sosipater and their men. With great cunning he begged them to let him go unharmed, arguing that he held the parents of most of them and the brothers of some as prisoners, and that harm might come to these.

**12:25** When he had given them full assurance of restoring them unharmed, they released him for the sake of saving their kinsmen.

**12:26** Judas then marched against Carnaim and the temple of Atargatis, and slaughtered twenty-five thousand persons.

**12:27** After the rout and destruction of these, he marched also against Ephron, a fortified town inhabited by large numbers of various peoples. Strong young men posted at the walls put up a vigorous resistance; inside were ample supplies of war engines and missiles.

**12:28** Calling upon the Sovereign who powerfully shatters the might of enemies, they took the city and slaughtered twenty-five thousand of its inhabitants.

**12:29** Moving on from there, they marched against Scythopolis, which lies six hundred stadia from Jerusalem.

**12:30** But the Jews settled there bore witness to the goodwill the Scythopolitans had shown them and their humane treatment during the times of distress.

**12:31** Having thanked them and exhorted them to continue showing kindness to the Jewish people in the future, they arrived in Jerusalem just as the feast of Weeks was at hand.

**12:32** After the festival called Pentecost, they advanced quickly against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea.

**12:33** Gorgias came out with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.

**12:34** When they engaged in battle, a small number of Jews fell.

**12:35** But a certain Dositheus, a horseman of Bacenor's company — a strong man — caught hold of Gorgias and gripped his cloak, dragging him off by force; and when a Thracian horseman rode up and cut off Dositheus's arm at the shoulder, Gorgias escaped to Marisa.

**12:36** As Esdris and his men had been fighting for a long time and were growing weary, Judas called on the Lord to appear as their ally and leader in the battle.

**12:37** Then, raising the battle cry in the Hebrew language and with hymns, he charged Gorgias's troops unexpectedly and put them to flight.

**12:38** Judas then rallied his army and came to the town of Adullam. As the seventh day was approaching, they purified themselves according to custom and kept the Sabbath there.

**12:39** On the following day — for it had by then become necessary — Judas's men went to collect the bodies of the fallen and bring them back to rest with their kindred in the ancestral tombs.

**12:40** But beneath the tunic of each of the fallen they found sacred tokens of the idols of Jamnia, which the law forbids the Jews to wear. It became evident to all that this was the reason these men had fallen.

**12:41** All then praised the Lord, the righteous judge, who makes hidden things manifest,

**12:42** and turned to prayer, beseeching that the sin that had been committed might be entirely blotted out. The noble Judas exhorted the people to keep themselves free from sin, having before their eyes what had happened on account of the sin of those who had fallen.

**12:43** He then took up a collection among the men, amounting to two thousand drachmas of silver, and sent it to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering — acting most excellently and nobly, with the resurrection of the dead in view.

**12:44** For if he had no expectation that the fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead.

**12:45** But if he looked to the splendid reward laid in store for those who fall asleep in godliness, the thought was holy and devout. Therefore he made atonement for the dead, so that they might be released from their sin.
